lessons.title: Water Supply Systems in African Buildings
lessons.body: This lesson introduces the practical design and installation of water supply systems in residential, commercial and institutional buildings across Africa. We begin with the reality that most African cities and towns face intermittent municipal supply, low pressure, and water quality variation. A plumber who understands these conditions can design systems that keep water flowing even when the mains fail. Start by assessing the source. Is it a municipal connection, a borehole, a rainwater tank, a river, or a tanker delivery? Each source has different pressure, quality and reliability. For municipal supply, always install a storage tank and a booster pump. The tank should be sized for at least one day of peak demand. For a typical three-bedroom home with four occupants, that is roughly 600 to 800 litres. For a small hotel with 20 rooms, plan for 4,000 to 6,000 litres. Use polyethylene or fibreglass tanks that resist algae and are easy to clean. Position the tank on a concrete slab above ground or on a strong roof structure. Never place a tank directly on the ground where it can be contaminated by runoff. The tank outlet should be at least 100 mm above the tank floor to allow sediment to settle. Install a first-flush diverter on rainwater systems and a floating suction line on all tanks to draw water from just below the surface, avoiding sludge. Pipe sizing is critical. In Africa, many plumbers use 20 mm or 25 mm pipes for everything, which causes pressure loss and noise. Use the following guide: 25 mm for a single bathroom, 32 mm for two bathrooms, 40 mm for three to four bathrooms, and 50 mm or larger for commercial kitchens and laundries. Always calculate the total fixture units and use a pressure loss table. Keep the velocity below 1.5 metres per second in cold water pipes and 1.2 metres per second in hot water pipes. Higher velocities cause erosion, noise and water hammer. For hot water, use PEX or CPVC in areas where copper is expensive or subject to theft. Copper is still excellent but must be protected from theft with locked enclosures or plastic-coated copper. Install isolation valves on every branch line so that a single leak does not shut down the whole building. Use gate valves for main lines and ball valves for fixture branches. Pressure management is the next key skill. Most African municipal pressures vary from 0.5 bar to 6 bar. Install a pressure reducing valve (PRV) after the tank or booster pump to keep building pressure between 2 and 3.5 bar. Higher pressure damages fixtures and wastes water. Lower pressure makes showers and washing machines useless. For multi-storey buildings, use a break tank and booster set on the roof or an intermediate floor. A typical booster set includes a pump, a pressure tank, a pressure switch and a non-return valve. Set the cut-in pressure at 1.5 bar and cut-out at 3.5 bar. Always install a bypass so the building can run on gravity if the pump fails. Water quality is not optional. In many African cities, municipal water is chlorinated but may still contain sediment. Borehole water may have iron, manganese, fluoride or bacteria. Install a sediment filter (5 micron) before the tank and a carbon filter after the tank for taste and odour. For boreholes, test for iron, manganese, fluoride, nitrate and coliforms. If iron is above 0.3 mg per litre, use an iron removal filter. If fluoride is above 1.5 mg per litre, use activated alumina or reverse osmosis. If bacteria are present, install an ultraviolet (UV) steriliser or dose the tank with chlorine at 0.5 mg per litre residual. Always keep a test kit on site. Maintenance is where most systems fail. Create a simple maintenance schedule: clean tanks every six months, replace sediment filters every three months, test chlorine residual weekly, check pump pressure monthly, and inspect for leaks every week. Train the client or caretaker to read the pressure gauge and to know the sound of a failing pump. Keep spare parts: a pressure switch, a non-return valve, a float valve, and a set of gaskets. Finally, document everything. Draw an as-built schematic showing tank, pump, PRV, filters, valves and pipe sizes. Label every valve. Give the client a folder with the schematic, maintenance schedule, and contact details. This professional approach wins repeat business and referrals. In Africa, word of mouth is the strongest marketing. A plumber who installs a system that works during water rationing will never lack work. Remember: design for failure of the mains, not for perfect supply. That single mindset separates a good plumber from a great one.

lessons.title: Drainage and Sanitation Systems for African Conditions
lessons.body: This lesson covers the design, installation and maintenance of drainage and sanitation systems in African buildings. Poor drainage is the cause of most plumbing complaints: slow drains, bad smells, blockages, and even structural damage. We will focus on practical solutions that work with local materials and labour. Start with the principle: drainage must move waste away quickly, without leaking, and without allowing sewer gas into the building. In Africa, many areas have no central sewer. You will install septic tanks, soakaways, or bio-digesters. For a typical household of six people, a septic tank should be at least 2,000 litres, with two chambers. The first chamber holds solids and the second allows further settling. The outlet goes to a soakaway or a drain field. Soakaways work only in sandy or loamy soil. In clay soil, you need a raised drain field or a mound system. Always test the soil with a percolation test: dig a hole 300 mm deep, fill with water, and see how long it takes to drain. If it drains slower than 25 mm per hour, do not use a soakaway. Use a mound or a constructed wetland instead. For commercial buildings, use a grease trap before the septic tank. A grease trap must be sized for the kitchen flow and cleaned weekly. If grease enters the drain field, it will clog the soil and the system will fail within a year. Pipe sizing for drainage is different from supply. Use 32 mm for washbasins, 40 mm for showers and sinks, 50 mm for bathtubs and washing machines, 75 mm for toilets, and 100 mm for main soil stacks. Always use 100 mm for the main line to the septic tank. Slope is critical. Use a fall of 1 in 60 for 100 mm pipes, 1 in 40 for 75 mm pipes, and 1 in 20 for 50 mm pipes. Too little slope causes solids to settle. Too much slope causes water to run away from solids, leaving them behind. Use a spirit level and a string line. Never guess. Ventilation is the most neglected part of African drainage. Every soil stack must extend above the roof by at least 300 mm and be fitted with a cowl or a vent cap. Every fixture must have a trap with a water seal of at least 50 mm. If a trap dries out, sewer gas enters the building. In hot climates, traps dry out quickly. Use trap primers or pour a cup of water into floor drains every week. For long drain runs, install an air admittance valve (AAV) at the highest point. AAVs are cheap and prevent vacuum that siphons traps. Inspection chambers are essential. Install one at every change of direction, at every junction, and every 15 metres on straight runs. Use 600 mm by 600 mm chambers with removable covers. In Africa, concrete rings or plastic chambers are common. Make sure the chamber is watertight and the cover is strong enough for traffic if in a driveway. For toilets, use low-flush or dual-flush models. A dual-flush toilet uses 3 to 6 litres per flush instead of 9 to 12 litres. This reduces the load on the septic tank and saves water. For public toilets, use squat pans with a foot-operated flush or a pour-flush pan. Pour-flush pans are common in West and East Africa and work well with low water supply. Always install a floor drain in every wet room. The floor must slope to the drain at 1 in 80. Use a stainless steel or plastic grate that can be removed for cleaning. In kitchens, install a grease trap and a floor drain with a solids basket. For laundry areas, install a lint trap before the drain. Maintenance is the difference between a system that lasts 20 years and one that fails in two. Provide the client with a simple schedule: pump the septic tank every 3 to 5 years, clean grease traps weekly, flush floor drains weekly, and inspect inspection chambers every six months. Teach the client what not to flush: sanitary pads, wet wipes, cooking oil, and chemicals that kill the bacteria in the septic tank. In many African cities, the biggest problem is illegal connections and stormwater entering the sanitary drain. Stormwater must go to a separate drain or soakaway. If stormwater enters the septic tank, it will overflow and cause pollution. Always separate storm and sanitary drains. For high water table areas, use a sealed septic tank and a pump chamber. The pump moves effluent to a raised drain field. For flood-prone areas, raise the inspection chamber covers above the flood level and use sealed covers. Finally, think about business. Drainage and sanitation work is often dirty and unpleasant, but it pays well because few plumbers want to do it. Specialise in septic tank installation, grease trap cleaning, and drain unblocking. Buy a drain cleaning machine and a set of rods. Offer a maintenance contract to hotels, schools and restaurants. A monthly visit to clean grease traps and check chambers can be a steady income. In Africa, reputation is everything. If you install a system that never smells and never blocks, you will be recommended to everyone. Always test your work: fill a bathtub and let it drain, flush all toilets at once, and run a hose into the floor drain. Check for leaks and gurgling. Fix any problem before you leave the site. That is the mark of a professional.

lessons.title: Hot Water Systems and Solar Water Heating in Africa
lessons.body: This lesson focuses on hot water systems, with special attention to solar water heating, which is the most practical and economical solution for most African climates. We will cover system types, sizing, installation, safety and maintenance. Start with the demand. A typical household of four people uses 30 to 50 litres of hot water per person per day. That is 120 to 200 litres per day. A small guesthouse with 10 rooms uses 1,000 to 1,500 litres per day. A hospital or school may use 3,000 litres or more. Always size the system for the morning peak, because most people shower between 6 and 8 am. For solar systems, you need to account for cloudy days. A well-insulated tank can keep water hot for 24 to 48 hours. In most of Africa, you get 4 to 6 peak sun hours per day. A 200-litre solar system with 2 square metres of collector area will heat 200 litres to 60 degrees Celsius on a sunny day. On a cloudy day, it may only reach 40 degrees. So always install a backup electric element or a gas booster. There are two main types of solar water heaters: flat plate and evacuated tube. Flat plate collectors are cheaper, more robust, and easier to repair. They work well in sunny areas with good direct radiation. Evacuated tube collectors are more efficient in cloudy or cold conditions, but they are more fragile and expensive. For most African homes, flat plate is the best choice. There are also two system types: thermosiphon and forced circulation. Thermosiphon relies on the fact that hot water rises. The tank must be above the collector. This is simple, reliable, and needs no pump. Forced circulation uses a pump and a controller. It is used when the tank is below the collector or when the collector is far from the tank. Forced circulation is more expensive and needs electricity, but it allows more flexible installation. For a typical African home, a thermosiphon system on the roof is ideal. Install the collector facing the equator: north in the southern hemisphere, south in the northern hemisphere. Tilt the collector at an angle equal to your latitude plus 10 degrees. For example, in Nairobi, latitude is about 1 degree south, so tilt at 10 to 15 degrees. In Johannesburg, latitude is 26 degrees south, so tilt at 35 to 40 degrees. This maximises year-round performance. Piping for hot water must be insulated. Use closed-cell foam insulation with a wall thickness of at least 20 mm. Insulate both the hot and cold pipes in the solar loop. Uninsulated pipes lose heat and can scald. Use copper or PEX for the solar loop. Copper is better for high temperatures, but PEX with an oxygen barrier is acceptable if the manufacturer rates it for solar. Never use PVC for hot water. It will soften and burst. Install a tempering valve or a thermostatic mixing valve at the outlet of the tank. This mixes hot and cold water to deliver a safe 50 to 55 degrees Celsius at the tap. Water above 60 degrees can cause third-degree burns in seconds, especially for children and the elderly. In hospitals and clinics, keep hot water storage at 60 degrees to kill Legionella bacteria, but deliver at 50 degrees at the point of use. Install a pressure relief valve on the tank and on the collector loop. Solar systems can generate high pressure if the water turns to steam. The relief valve must discharge to a safe drain. Never block or cap a relief valve. Install a non-return valve on the cold inlet to prevent hot water from flowing back into the cold supply. Install a vacuum breaker on the collector loop to prevent back-siphonage. For freeze protection, in highland areas like the Ethiopian highlands, Lesotho, or the Drakensberg, use a closed-loop system with antifreeze or a drain-back system. In most of tropical Africa, freeze is not a concern. Maintenance is simple but essential. Check the collector glass for cracks or dirt. Clean it every month with water and a soft brush. Check the insulation for damage. Check the tank for scale. In hard water areas, descale the tank every year with a mild acid solution. Check the sacrificial anode in the tank every two years and replace it if it is more than 50 percent consumed. Check the pump and controller on forced circulation systems every three months. Check the pressure relief valve by lifting the lever every six months. For electric backup, check the element and thermostat every year. For gas backup, check the burner and flue every year. Safety is paramount. Never install a solar system on a roof that cannot support the weight. A 200-litre tank full of water weighs over 250 kg. Spread the load over at least two rafters. Use stainless steel straps or galvanised brackets. Never use mild steel that will rust. For lightning protection, bond the collector frame to the building earthing system. In areas with frequent lightning, install a lightning rod nearby. For business, solar water heating is a growing market in Africa. Many countries have tax incentives or rebates. You can offer a package: supply, install, and maintain. Train your staff on solar installation. Get certified if possible. Offer a five-year warranty on the collector and a two-year warranty on the tank. Keep spare parts: vacuum tubes, flat plate absorbers, controllers, pumps, and thermostats. Market to guesthouses, schools, clinics, and middle-class homes. Show them the savings: a solar system can cut electricity bills by 40 to 60 percent. In many African countries, electricity is expensive and unreliable. Solar hot water is a smart investment. Finally, always commission the system properly. Fill the tank, check for leaks, run the pump, check the temperature rise, and set the controller. Show the client how to read the temperature gauge and how to switch to backup. Give them a manual and your contact number. A well-installed solar water heater will last 15 to 20 years and will be a constant advertisement for your business.

lessons.title: Pipe Materials, Fittings and Jointing for African Plumbers
lessons.body: This lesson covers the practical selection and use of pipe materials, fittings, and jointing methods in African plumbing. Choosing the right material saves money, prevents leaks, and ensures a long-lasting installation. We will compare the common materials, explain where each is best used, and show how to make reliable joints. Start with the most common material: uPVC (unplasticised polyvinyl chloride). It is cheap, easy to cut, and resistant to corrosion. Use uPVC for cold water supply and drainage. It is not suitable for hot water. uPVC comes in different pressure ratings: 6 bar, 10 bar, and 16 bar. For buried mains, use 10 bar or 16 bar. For above-ground drainage, use 6 bar or drainage-grade pipe. Always use the correct solvent cement. Clean the pipe and fitting with a cleaner, apply cement to both surfaces, push together with a quarter turn, and hold for 30 seconds. Do not use too much cement. Do not use cement on wet surfaces. In hot climates, uPVC expands and contracts. Allow for expansion by using expansion joints or by leaving a small gap in long runs. Never use uPVC for compressed air or gas. Next is CPVC (chlorinated polyvinyl chloride). It handles hot water up to 90 degrees Celsius. It is more expensive than uPVC but cheaper than copper. Use CPVC for hot water supply in homes and small commercial buildings. It is joined with solvent cement, similar to uPVC. Use the correct CPVC cement. Do not mix uPVC and CPVC cement. CPVC is more brittle than uPVC, so handle it carefully. Do not use it where it will be exposed to sunlight for long periods unless it is painted or wrapped. PEX (cross-linked polyethylene) is the most popular material for hot and cold water in new African buildings. It is flexible, cheap, and easy to install. It comes in coils and can be run through walls and floors with few fittings. PEX is joined with crimp rings, clamp rings, or push-fit fittings. Use a crimping tool and a go/no-go gauge to check the crimp. Push-fit fittings are fast but more expensive. PEX is resistant to freeze damage because it expands. It is also resistant to scale. However, PEX can be damaged by UV light, so keep it out of direct sunlight. PEX is not allowed in some countries for certain applications, so check local codes. Copper is the traditional material for hot and cold water. It is durable, handles high temperatures, and is recyclable. But copper is expensive and is often stolen in Africa. If you use copper, protect it with locked enclosures or use plastic-coated copper. Copper is joined with soldering or press fittings. Soldering requires a torch, flux, and lead-free solder. Press fittings require a press tool. For small jobs, soldering is fine. For large jobs, press fittings are faster and safer. Copper can corrode in acidic water. If the pH is below 6.5, use plastic instead. Copper is also affected by high chloride levels. In coastal areas, use copper-nickel or plastic. Galvanised steel is still common in older buildings. It is strong but corrodes from the inside. It is joined with threaded fittings and Teflon tape or pipe dope. Galvanised steel is difficult to repair and should be replaced with PEX or CPVC when possible. If you must join galvanised to copper, use a dielectric union to prevent galvanic corrosion. Never connect copper directly to galvanised steel. HDPE (high-density polyethylene) is used for buried water mains and borehole pipes. It is joined with compression fittings or fusion welding. Fusion welding is the best method for large pipes. It requires a fusion machine. For small pipes, compression fittings are fine. HDPE is flexible and can be pulled through trenches. It is resistant to chemicals and abrasion. It is not suitable for hot water. For drainage, uPVC is the standard. For underground drainage, use uPVC or HDPE. For soil and waste, use uPVC with rubber ring joints or solvent joints. Rubber ring joints are faster and allow for movement. Solvent joints are stronger and watertight. For vent pipes, use uPVC. For rainwater, use uPVC or HDPE. For gutters, use uPVC, aluminium, or galvanised steel. In Africa, uPVC gutters are popular because they do not rust. Fittings are as important as pipes. Use the correct fitting for the job. Elbows, tees, couplings, reducers, and adaptors must match the pipe material and size. Never force a fitting. Never use too many fittings. Every fitting adds friction and a potential leak. Use long-radius elbows for drainage to reduce blockage. Use sweep tees instead of sanitary tees where possible. For supply, use full-flow ball valves and gate valves. For drainage, use inspection eyes and access caps. Jointing is a skill. For solvent cement joints, follow the manufacturer instructions. For threaded joints, use Teflon tape or pipe dope. Wrap Teflon tape clockwise around the threads. Do not use too much. For compression joints, tighten by hand plus one quarter turn with a wrench. Do not overtighten. For push-fit joints, mark the insertion depth and push until it clicks. Pull back to check. For crimp joints, use the correct tool and check with a gauge. Always pressure test after installation. For water supply, test at 1.5 times the working pressure for one hour. For drainage, test with water and check for leaks. For buried pipes, test before backfilling. Take photos of the installation before covering. Give the client a diagram. In Africa, material availability varies. Sometimes you must use what is available. But always choose the best material you can afford. Cheap pipes fail early and cost more in repairs. Buy from reputable suppliers. Check for the manufacturer mark and the pressure rating. Avoid second-hand pipes. Avoid pipes that are faded or cracked. Store pipes out of direct sunlight. Keep them clean. Use end caps to prevent dirt and insects. Finally, think about the business. Offer different packages: economy (uPVC and PEX), standard (CPVC and PEX), and premium (copper and PEX). Explain the pros and cons to the client. Show them the warranty. Keep a stock of common fittings on your van. Train your apprentices on all materials. A plumber who can work with any material is more valuable. In Africa, the best plumbers are those who can adapt. They know when to use local materials and when to insist on quality. They never compromise on safety. They always test their work. That is how you build a reputation that lasts.

lessons.title: Business Skills and Customer Service for African Plumbers
lessons.body: This lesson is about the business side of plumbing. Many African plumbers are excellent technicians but struggle to make a profit because they do not manage money, time, or customers well. We will cover pricing, quoting, invoicing, record keeping, marketing, and customer service. The goal is to turn your skill into a sustainable business that supports your family and creates jobs. Start with pricing. The biggest mistake is to guess a price. You must know your costs. Calculate your hourly rate. Add up your monthly costs: transport, fuel, tools, insurance, phone, rent, and your own salary. Divide by the number of billable hours you work per month. For example, if your costs are 10,000 shillings per month and you work 100 billable hours, your cost rate is 100 shillings per hour. Add a profit margin of 20 to 30 percent. So your hourly rate is 120 to 130 shillings. For a job, estimate the hours and add materials. Always add 10 percent for waste and unexpected problems. Never quote a fixed price without seeing the job. Go to the site. Measure. Take photos. Ask questions. Then write a quote. A quote should include: your business name, client name, date, description of work, materials list with prices, labour cost, total, payment terms, and validity period. Use a simple template. Print it or send it by WhatsApp. Keep a copy. For small jobs, you can give a verbal quote, but always confirm in writing. For large jobs, ask for a deposit of 30 to 50 percent. Never start work without a deposit. This protects you from clients who refuse to pay. For materials, buy from a supplier who gives you a trade discount. Negotiate. Buy in bulk for common items. Keep receipts. For invoicing, use a simple invoice book or a phone app. Include the same details as the quote. Mark it paid when the client pays. Give a receipt. Keep a record of all income and expenses. Use a notebook or a spreadsheet. At the end of each month, calculate your profit. If you are not making a profit, raise your prices or cut your costs. Do not work for free. Time management is critical. Plan your day. Group jobs by area to save fuel. Call clients before you go to confirm. Arrive on time. If you are delayed, call. Do not overbook. Allow extra time for traffic and for unexpected problems. Keep your tools organised. A messy van wastes time. Keep a checklist for each job: tools, materials, safety gear, and paperwork. Customer service is your best marketing. In Africa, people trust people they know. Be polite. Be clean. Wear a uniform if possible. Introduce yourself. Explain what you are doing. Listen to the client. Do not argue. If you make a mistake, admit it and fix it. Do not blame the client or the materials. Always clean up after the job. Leave the site cleaner than you found it. Show the client how to use the new system. Give them a maintenance schedule. Follow up after a week to check everything is fine. Ask for a referral. Offer a discount for referrals. Use WhatsApp to stay in touch. Send reminders for maintenance. Build a database of clients. Send them a message on their birthday or during holidays. This keeps you in their mind. Marketing does not have to be expensive. Word of mouth is the best. Ask satisfied clients to recommend you. Join a local business association. Attend trade shows. Put a sign on your van. Create a simple business card. Use social media: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp status. Post photos of your work. Show before and after. Ask clients for reviews. Respond to every review, even negative ones. Be professional. For larger contracts, you need to bid. Learn to read drawings and bills of quantities. Work with an architect or engineer. Get a copy of the tender documents. Ask questions. Submit your bid on time. Include all costs. Do not underbid. If you win, sign a contract. Read the contract carefully. Understand payment terms, penalties, and retention. For public tenders, you may need to register your business and get a tax compliance certificate. Do that. It opens doors. Manage your money. Open a bank account. Separate business and personal money. Pay yourself a salary. Save for taxes. In many African countries, you must pay VAT or sales tax if your turnover is above a threshold. Register. Pay on time. Avoid fines. Keep records for at least five years. Use a simple accounting system. If you cannot afford an accountant, use a bookkeeper or a phone app. Save for emergencies. Plumbing is seasonal. During the rainy season, there may be less work. Save during the dry season. Invest in tools. Buy good tools. They last longer and make you faster. Insure your tools and your vehicle. Train your staff. Send them to courses. Pay them fairly. Give them incentives for good work. Treat them with respect. A happy team works harder and stays with you. Finally, think about growth. You can move from a one-man operation to a company. Hire apprentices. Train them. Delegate. Focus on getting more clients. Offer new services: solar water heating, borehole installation, septic tank cleaning, leak detection. Specialise in a niche. Become the expert. In Africa, the demand for plumbing services is growing. Cities are expanding. People are building homes. Hotels, schools, and hospitals need maintenance. If you run your business professionally, you will succeed. Remember: your reputation is your most valuable asset. Protect it. Do good work. Charge fairly. Pay your bills. Treat people well. The money will follow.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Plumbing Trade Standards, Water Quality and Site Data for African Plumbers

This Practical Reference lesson is the working companion to the other four modules in the RISE AFRICA Plumbing course. It gathers the numbers, standards and field checks that a plumber needs on site every day: how much water a household actually uses, what pressure and flow a system must deliver, what water quality limits apply, and how to price and document work so the business survives. In most African markets the plumber is not only the installer but also the technical advisor, the quality controller and often the person who certifies that a supply is safe to drink. Getting the figures right is therefore both a health issue and a commercial one: a job that fails because of undersized pipes, wrong gradient or contaminated storage will cost far more in callbacks and lost reputation than the original installation was worth.

The guidance below is drawn from published, freely available sources: the FAO On-farm irrigation and water supply guidance, the WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality and Water Safety in Buildings, and the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) service ladders. National plumbing codes across Africa (Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania, Ghana, Uganda) follow broadly similar principles, so the reference values here can be adapted locally with the authority having jurisdiction.

Table 1. Typical household water demand and storage sizing for African conditions

Use Table 1 to size tanks and pipes before you quote. A common error in African installations is to size storage on the number of taps rather than on occupancy and peak demand. For a family of six in an urban compound with a WC and shower, 150 L/person/day gives 900 L/day; a 1,000â2,000 L tank gives one to two days of autonomy and rides out the frequent mains interruptions that characterise many municipal supplies.

Table 2. Field reference values for pressure, gradient and pipe sizing

Drainage fall (110 mm soil pipe)1:60 to 1:100 (1â1.7%)Too flat blocks; too steep drains water faster than solidsWHO Water Safety in Buildings (2011)

Hot water pipe velocity0.5â1.2 m/sLimits erosion-corrosion and heat lossWHO Water Safety in Buildings (2011)
Minimum pipe diameter, main supply to house20â25 mm (Â¾â1 in) for small homes; 32â50 mm for multi-unitUndersizing is the most common cause of poor pressureNational plumbing codes
Storage tank turnoverComplete turnover within 24â48 hoursStagnant water grows biofilm and LegionellaWHO Water Safety in Buildings (2011)
Free chlorine residual at tap0.2â0.5 mg/L (WHO guidance); 0.5 mg/L at point of delivery in many national standardsIndicates adequate disinfection and no recontaminationWHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (2022)
â  SAFETY WARNING â WATER QUALITY AND CHEMICALS

Water supplied to a building is not automatically safe to drink. Storage tanks, dead legs, cross-connections and backflow are the leading causes of contamination in African buildings. Never connect a mains supply directly to a cistern, hose or irrigation line without an air gap or a verified backflow preventer. When chlorinating a tank or pipework, use only approved chlorine products, follow the manufacturer's dose, wear gloves and eye protection, ventilate the area, and flush thoroughly before the water is used. Do not use lead-based solder, lead pipes or unapproved plastic on drinking-water lines. If a supply smells, is discoloured, or tests positive for E. coli, stop work, notify the client in writing, and do not certify the installation until the water is safe. Refer to WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (2022) and national public health authority requirements.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Demand first, pipe second. Count occupants and fittings, apply Table 1, then size pipes and tank. Never size by number of taps alone.
  2. Pressure at the furthest outlet. Test with a gauge at the worst-case tap; confirm at least 1.0 bar with all other outlets closed, and check it again with two taps open.
  3. Gradient and venting. Confirm drainage falls at 1:60 to 1:100, every trap is vented, and no branch exceeds the code maximum length without a vent.
  4. Backflow protection. Fit a non-return valve or air gap at every cross-connection, including hosepipes, boilers, cisterns and irrigation points.
  5. Tank hygiene. Tanks must be covered, insect-proof, opaque or shaded, with a screened overflow and a drain-down valve. Clean and disinfect at least every six months.
  6. Test and record. Record free chlorine residual, pH and, where required, bacteriological results. Give the client a signed commissioning sheet with pressures, flow rates and test results.
  7. Materials. Use only approved pipe, fittings and jointing compounds for potable water; keep a materials schedule in every quote so substitutions are visible.
  8. Price the risk. Include a call-back allowance, a water-test line item and a written scope in every quotation; document variations in writing before doing the work.

Business-first notes for African plumbers

Every figure in this lesson is a selling point. A plumber who arrives with a pressure gauge, a chlorine test kit and a commissioning sheet looks like a professional and can charge for a service, not just a repair. In markets where most competitors quote verbally and informally, a written scope with the demand calculation attached is a competitive advantage. Use Table 1 to justify tank size to the client, Table 2 to justify pipe diameter, and the checklist as the basis of a maintenance contract â quarterly tank cleaning, annual pressure testing and water-quality checks. These recurring services are where the sustainable income lies, far more than one-off installations.

Keep a simple job file for each client: site sketch, demand calculation, materials used, test results, photos of the installation before closing up walls, and the commissioning sheet. When a dispute arises â and in informal construction markets it often does â this file is your evidence. It also becomes your portfolio when you bid for larger work such as schools, clinics and small hotels, where clients increasingly require documented water safety management. Align your practice with the WHO water safety plan approach: identify hazards, control them at the point of installation, and monitor with simple field tests. That is the difference between a plumber and a water safety professional.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a vent pipe in a plumbing drainage system?
options: A) To supply hot water to fixtures
B) To equalize air pressure and allow gases to escape
C) To filter debris from wastewater
D) To increase water flow pressure
quiz.explanation: Vent pipes equalize pressure in the drainage system and allow sewer gases to escape safely through the roof.

quiz.q: Which material is most commonly used for residential water supply lines today?
quiz.explanation: Copper and PEX are the most common modern materials for residential water supply lines due to durability and ease of installation.

quiz.q: What does the term fixture unit refer to in plumbing?
options: A) The number of fixtures in a building
B) A measure of the load a fixture places on the drainage system
C) The cost of installing a fixture
D) The warranty period of a fixture
quiz.explanation: A fixture unit is a measure of the probable discharge rate or load a plumbing fixture places on the drainage system.

quiz.q: What is the minimum slope typically required for a horizontal drain pipe of 3 inches or less?
quiz.explanation: A slope of 1/4 inch per foot is the standard minimum for horizontal drain pipes 3 inches or less in diameter.

quiz.q: Which device prevents backflow of contaminated water into a potable water supply?
quiz.explanation: A backflow preventer stops contaminated water from reversing into the potable water supply, protecting public health.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a P-trap under a sink?
options: B) To create a water seal that blocks sewer gases
quiz.explanation: A P-trap holds a water seal that prevents sewer gases from entering the building through the drain.

quiz.q: Which type of pipe is best suited for underground drainage and sewer lines?
quiz.explanation: PVC and ABS plastic pipes are commonly used for underground drainage and sewer lines due to corrosion resistance and durability.

quiz.q: What should a plumber do first before repairing a water heater?
options: D) Shut off the power and water supply
quiz.explanation: Before repairing a water heater, always shut off the power and water supply to ensure safety and prevent damage.

quiz.q: Which water supply system is most common in rapidly growing African urban areas with intermittent municipal supply?
options: B) Rooftop storage tank with booster pump
C) Underground reservoir with no pump
D) Gravity supply from distant hills
quiz.explanation: Rooftop tanks and booster pumps help maintain pressure when municipal supply is intermittent.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a break pressure tank in an African gravity water supply system?
options: B) Reduce pressure to safe levels
quiz.explanation: Break pressure tanks reduce high static pressure in gravity-fed lines to protect pipes and fittings.

quiz.q: In African buildings, why is a twin or dual water supply system sometimes installed?
options: A) To separate potable and non-potable water
quiz.explanation: Dual systems keep potable water separate from water used for flushing or irrigation.

quiz.q: Which drainage system is best suited to areas with heavy seasonal rainfall and poor municipal sewerage in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Septic tanks with soakaways are common where public sewers are unavailable or unreliable.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a vent pipe in an African building drainage system?
options: B) Equalize pressure and release gases
C) Increase water flow to taps
quiz.explanation: Vent pipes prevent trap siphonage and allow foul gases to escape safely.

quiz.q: Why are grease traps important in African commercial kitchens?
options: B) They prevent fats from blocking drains
quiz.explanation: Grease traps intercept fats and oils that would otherwise clog drainage pipes.

quiz.q: Which hot water system is most practical for sunny African regions with unreliable electricity?
options: B) Solar water heater with electric backup
quiz.explanation: Solar water heating with electric backup uses abundant sunshine and ensures hot water during cloudy periods.

quiz.q: What is a key maintenance task for solar water heating systems in dusty African environments?
options: A) Painting the tank black monthly
quiz.explanation: Dust reduces solar collector efficiency, so regular cleaning is essential.

quiz.q: Which pipe material is most resistant to corrosion in African soils with high salinity?
quiz.explanation: uPVC is highly resistant to corrosion and is widely used in aggressive soil conditions.

quiz.q: Why is PPR pipe increasingly popular for hot water plumbing in African buildings?
options: A) It is the cheapest material
B) It handles heat and pressure well
D) It is flexible like rubber
quiz.explanation: PPR pipes withstand hot water temperatures and pressures and are easy to joint by heat fusion.

quiz.q: What is the correct method for jointing HDPE pipes in African water projects?
quiz.explanation: HDPE pipes are typically joined by butt fusion or electrofusion for strong leak-free joints.

quiz.q: Which fitting is used to connect pipes of different diameters?
quiz.explanation: Reducers join pipes of different sizes in a plumbing system.

quiz.q: Why should African plumbers prepare a written quotation for customers?
options: B) To clearly state scope, price and terms
C) To avoid doing the work
quiz.explanation: A written quotation builds trust and prevents disputes by clarifying scope and cost.

quiz.q: What is good customer service for an African plumber arriving at a client site?
options: B) Arrive on time and explain the work
quiz.explanation: Punctuality and clear communication improve customer satisfaction and repeat business.

quiz.q: Which record should a professional African plumber keep for each job?
options: B) Job details, materials used and warranty
quiz.explanation: Job records support follow-up, warranty claims and business planning.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum pressure for a domestic water supply in African buildings?
quiz.explanation: About 1.0 bar at fixtures is generally needed for satisfactory flow.

quiz.q: Which device protects a hot water cylinder from excessive pressure?
quiz.explanation: A pressure relief valve opens to release excess pressure and prevent cylinder explosion.

quiz.q: In an African context, what is a common cause of blocked drains in residential areas?
options: B) Solid waste and sand entering drains
quiz.explanation: Solid waste, sand and debris frequently block drains where maintenance is poor.

quiz.q: Which test is used to check for leaks in a new plumbing installation?
quiz.explanation: A pressure test detects leaks by holding water or air under pressure in the pipes.

quiz.q: Why is a non-return valve installed on a booster pump discharge in African buildings?
options: B) To prevent backflow into mains
quiz.explanation: A non-return valve stops contaminated water from flowing back into the supply.

quiz.q: What should an African plumber do before starting work in a customer home?
options: A) Turn off water and power if needed
quiz.explanation: Isolating water and power ensures safety before plumbing work begins.

quiz.q: Which document helps an African plumber calculate fair labour and material charges?
options: A) A price list and job estimate
quiz.explanation: A price list and estimate help ensure fair and consistent charges for labour and materials.
